Q: What does a crimper do in copper cabling work?
Option1: Seats wires into insulation displacement connector (IDC) slots on a patch panel
Option2: Attaches modular connectors (for example, RJ-45) to the ends of twisted-pair cable by compressing the contacts
Option3: Locates a cable in a bundle using an audible tone

Q: What is the purpose of a cable stripper?
Option1: Remove the outer jacket of a cable without damaging the inner conductors
Option2: Test end-to-end continuity

Q: What does a WiFi analyzer help you determine?
Option2: Radio signal strength, channel utilization, and interference sources for wireless networks
Option3: Which cables are open or shorted

Q: What tool pair is commonly used to trace an unlabelled copper cable through walls or bundles?
Option2: Punchdown tool and crimper

Q: What is the function of a punchdown tool?
Option1: Crimps RJ-45 plugs to cable ends
Option2: Seats individual wires into insulation displacement connector (IDC) slots on 66 or 110 blocks or keystone jacks, trimming excess

Q: What is a cable tester used for?
Option2: Validating copper pair mapping and continuity; detecting opens, shorts, and miswires
Option3: Provisioning Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) scopes

Q: What does a loopback plug do?
Option1: Bridges transmit to receive on a port to verify the interface or network interface card (NIC) and link electronics
Option2: Repeats wireless signals

Q: What is a network tap?
Option1: A device that passively copies network traffic for analysis without interrupting flow
Option2: A device that injects power into Ethernet

Q: Which tool should you use first when making a custom Category 6 patch cable?
Option2: Cable stripper to remove the jacket

Q: Which tool is best to terminate horizontal cabling into a patch panel?
Option2: Punchdown tool

Q: Which scenario calls for a toner and probe set?
Option1: Validating that pairs are correctly terminated on a new jack
Option2: Finding the far end of an unlabelled cable behind a wall
Option4: Testing an Ethernet adapter on a laptop without a switch

Q: Which scenario is ideal for a loopback plug?
Option2: Testing whether a network interface card (NIC) can establish link and pass a built-in self-test

Q: What can a basic cable tester NOT verify that a certifier can?
Option2: Correct pinout
Option3: Performance parameters like attenuation and near-end crosstalk to a standards limit

Q: Which statement compares crimper and punchdown tools correctly?
Option2: Crimper attaches modular plugs to cable ends; punchdown seats individual wires into insulation displacement connector (IDC) blocks or keystones
Option3: Crimper is for fiber; punchdown is for coax

Q: Which tool directly helps plan access point channel assignments?
Option2: WiFi analyzer

Q: A newly installed jack fails continuity on pairs 3 and 6. Which tool fixes this most directly?
Option2: Punchdown tool to reseat wires into insulation displacement connector (IDC) slots

Q: You built a patch cable and want to confirm T568B pinout and continuity. Which tool set is best?
Option2: Toner and probe

Q: You need to capture real production traffic for intrusion analysis without affecting the live link. Best choice?
Option2: Switch port in access mode

Q: A user claims WiFi is slow at lunchtime. Which tool gives evidence to choose new channels?
Option2: WiFi analyzer showing channel utilization and interference

Q: You suspect an office cable bundle is mislabeled. Which workflow is best?
Option1: Use a WiFi analyzer to scan channels
Option2: Attach a tone generator to the suspected jack and follow the sound with the inductive probe at the patch panel
Option3: Crimp new plugs on every cable
Option4: Install a network tap on each run

Option2: Attach a loopback plug to the NIC and check for link activity or run NIC diagnostics

Option2: Certification grade cable analyzer that measures parameters such as attenuation and near-end crosstalk
